body:
Meaning and foundations of classical music

Indian classical music is a traditional system of music governed by established principles of melody and rhythm. It has developed over many centuries through religious practices, scholarly traditions, royal patronage and the transmission of musical knowledge from teachers to disciples.

Indian music broadly includes classical music and folk music. Classical music follows established musical frameworks, while folk music develops primarily through the customs, occupations, festivals and social life of particular communities. Both traditions influence each other.

Vedic roots

Among the 4 Vedas, the Sama Veda is particularly associated with music. Its verses are arranged for melodic chanting during religious rituals. Vedic chanting represents an important early foundation of Indian musical traditions, although modern classical music developed through many subsequent historical stages.

Essential musical concepts

Swara

A swara is a musical note. Indian classical music recognises 7 basic swaras, collectively known as Saptak when arranged within an octave.

Short nameFull name
SaShadja
ReRishabha
GaGandhara
MaMadhyama
PaPanchama
DhaDhaivata
NiNishada

Sa and Pa are regarded as fixed notes within the traditional system, while the other notes have recognised variants. The actual pitch of Sa is selected according to the singer or instrument.

Raga

A raga is a melodic framework within which a musician develops a musical composition or improvisation. It specifies characteristic notes, their relationships and characteristic melodic movements.

A raga is more than a scale. Two ragas may use similar notes but remain distinct because their characteristic movements and musical emphasis differ.

  • Aroha: The ascending arrangement of notes.
  • Avaroha: The descending arrangement of notes.
  • Vadi: The principal or most important note in a raga in Hindustani theory.
  • Samvadi: The note of secondary importance in relation to the vadi.

Tala and laya

Tala is an organised rhythmic cycle containing a specified number of beats. Each cycle repeats throughout the rhythmically measured portion of a musical composition.

For example, the Hindustani rhythmic cycle known as Teental contains 16 beats.

Laya refers to the speed or tempo of musical movement. Its broad categories are Vilambit (slow), Madhya (medium) and Drut (fast).

Raga governs melodic development, tala governs rhythmic organisation, and laya governs speed. Changing the tempo does not necessarily change the tala.

Drone and improvisation

A drone provides a continuous tonal reference against which the melody develops. The tanpura, also called tambura, commonly performs this function.

Improvisation allows musicians to develop new melodic or rhythmic passages within established musical rules. It is an important feature of both Hindustani and Carnatic classical music.

Prelims focus

  • The Sama Veda is particularly associated with musical chanting.
  • Indian classical music recognises 7 basic swaras.
  • Raga is a melodic framework; tala is a rhythmic cycle.
  • Teental contains 16 beats.
  • The tanpura primarily provides a drone.
  • Trap: Tala and laya are related but are not interchangeable terms.

[References: Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Social Science, Standard 10, English edition, 2020 reprint, Chapter 2, Music, p. 12 (online edition consulted in place of the English compendium; corresponding Gujarati chapter consulted in the project); NIOS, Indian Culture and Heritage, Secondary Course 223, Chapter 12, sections 12.1–12.3; Darbar, Glossary of Indian Music Terms; Metropolitan Museum of Art, Musical Instruments of the Indian Subcontinent. Online sources consulted 25 November 2026.]

title: Foundations of Indian Classical Music: Swara, Raga and Tala

body:
The 2 major classical traditions

Indian classical music has 2 principal systems: Hindustani music and Carnatic music, also spelled Karnatik music. Both developed from older Indian musical traditions and share the fundamental concepts of swara, raga and tala.

During the medieval period, differences in regional languages, religious traditions, royal patronage and cultural interaction gradually contributed to their emergence as distinct musical systems. Their development cannot be attributed to a single individual or a single historical event.

Hindustani music

Hindustani classical music developed predominantly in northern India. Its historical development reflects indigenous Indian musical traditions as well as interaction with Persian and Central Asian cultural traditions, particularly during the Delhi Sultanate and Mughal periods.

Royal courts, devotional institutions and hereditary musical families contributed to its development. The gharana system became an important means of preserving and transmitting different styles of Hindustani music.

Carnatic music

Carnatic classical music developed predominantly in southern India, particularly in present-day Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Kerala.

It has strong historical connections with temple traditions, devotional compositions and South Indian royal courts. Its repertoire includes compositions in Telugu, Sanskrit, Tamil, Kannada and other languages.

Comparison of the 2 systems

FeatureHindustaniCarnatic
Principal regionNorthern IndiaSouthern India
Major vocal formsDhrupad, Khayal, TaranaKriti, Varnam, Tillana
Parent-scale classification10 thaats72 melakartas
Typical melodic instrumentsSitar, Sarod, SarangiVeena, Violin
Typical percussionTabla, PakhawajMridangam, Ghatam
TransmissionGharanas and teacher-disciple lineagesTeacher-disciple lineages and compositional traditions

These are characteristic associations rather than exclusive rules. For example, the flute, violin and tanpura can be used in both systems.

Thaat and melakarta

A thaat is a parent-scale framework used to classify Hindustani ragas. Pandit Vishnu Narayan Bhatkhande systematised an influential classification of Hindustani ragas into 10 thaats during the early 20th century.

A melakarta is a parent raga in the Carnatic system. The theoretical foundation of the 72-mela classification is associated with Venkatamakhin, the 17th-century author of Chaturdandi Prakashika. The system subsequently underwent further development.

Carnatic ragas are commonly classified as parent ragas, called Janaka ragas, and derived ragas, called Janya ragas.

The numbers 10 and 72 refer to parent classification systems, not to the total number of ragas available in either tradition.

Composition and improvisation

Hindustani music often places considerable emphasis on the gradual development of a raga. Carnatic music is particularly rich in structured compositions, including kritis by major composers.

However, both traditions combine established compositions with improvisation. It is incorrect to describe Hindustani music as entirely improvised or Carnatic music as entirely predetermined.

Prelims focus

  • Hindustani music developed predominantly in northern India.
  • Carnatic music developed predominantly in southern India.
  • Bhatkhande is associated with the 10-thaat classification.
  • Venkatamakhin is associated with the theoretical development of the 72-mela system.
  • Both traditions use raga, tala and improvisation.
  • Trap: The use of a particular instrument is not necessarily exclusive to one classical tradition.

[References: NIOS, Indian Culture and Heritage, Secondary Course 223, Chapter 12, sections 12.1–12.3, pp. 170–173; Centre for Cultural Resources and Training, Performing Arts, Indian Classical Music; IGNCA, Ragalaksana Sri, discussion of Venkatamakhin and mela classification; SATHEE, IIT Kanpur, Classical Music; Metropolitan Museum of Art, Musical Instruments of the Indian Subcontinent. Consulted 25 November 2026.]

title: Hindustani and Carnatic Music: Common Foundations and Major Differences

body:
Major forms of Hindustani vocal music

A musical form is an established manner of organising and presenting a composition. Hindustani vocal forms differ in their historical development, treatment of ragas, rhythmic organisation and emphasis on lyrics.

Dhrupad

Dhrupad is among the oldest surviving major forms of Hindustani classical vocal music. It developed through devotional traditions and received considerable patronage in medieval royal courts.

It is characterised by a dignified presentation, carefully developed ragas and a relatively restrained approach to ornamentation. Its compositions may express devotion, philosophical ideas or praise of rulers.

The pakhawaj is traditionally associated with Dhrupad accompaniment. Tansen and Swami Haridas are important historical figures associated with this tradition.

Dhamar

Dhamar is closely associated with the Dhrupad tradition. Its compositions frequently concern the celebration of Holi and the playful relationship between Krishna and Radha.

The rhythmic cycle called Dhamar Tala contains 14 beats. Pakhawaj accompaniment is traditional in this form.

Khayal

The word Khayal means imagination or thought. Khayal allows considerable freedom in melodic development and improvisation within the framework of a raga.

It became a dominant form of Hindustani classical vocal music. Compared with Dhrupad, it generally allows greater melodic ornamentation and flexibility.

Khayal developed over a long historical period. Its development should not be reduced to an unqualified claim that a single medieval musician invented the form.

Tarana

Tarana is a classical vocal form distinguished by its characteristic rhythmic syllables, such as tana, dere and na. Its syllables generally receive greater emphasis than the narrative meaning of ordinary lyrics.

Amir Khusro is traditionally associated with the development of Tarana, although its exact historical origin is not conclusively established.

Related semi-classical and devotional forms

Thumri

Thumri is a semi-classical vocal form that places particular emphasis on emotional expression and the meaning of poetic lyrics. Its themes frequently concern love, separation and devotion, including compositions about Radha and Krishna.

Lucknow and Banaras are historically important centres of Thumri.

Tappa

Tappa is a semi-classical form distinguished by rapid and intricate melodic movement. It developed from folk singing traditions associated with Punjab and is traditionally linked with the songs of camel riders.

Shori Mian is credited with developing Tappa as a cultivated musical form.

Qawwali and Ghazal

Qawwali is a devotional musical form particularly associated with Sufi traditions. It has an important place in Chishti religious gatherings and is commonly performed by groups of singers.

Ghazal is primarily a poetic form consisting of couplets, which may also be presented musically. Its themes include love, separation, philosophical reflection and spirituality.

Dhrupad, Khayal and Tarana are principal Hindustani classical forms. Thumri and Tappa are generally classified as semi-classical forms, while Qawwali is especially associated with Sufi devotion.

Prelims focus

  • Dhrupad is an old classical vocal form traditionally accompanied by pakhawaj.
  • Dhamar Tala has 14 beats and is associated with Holi compositions.
  • Khayal allows extensive imaginative development of a raga.
  • Tarana is distinguished by rhythmic syllables.
  • Thumri emphasises lyrical and emotional expression; Tappa is associated with Punjab.
  • Trap: Qawwali belongs to the Sufi devotional tradition and is not synonymous with Khayal or Dhrupad.

[References: NIOS, Indian Culture and Heritage, Secondary Course 223, Chapter 12, Performing Arts: Music, Dance and Drama, pp. 170–173; Darbar, Hindustani Vocals and Glossary of Indian Music Terms; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Class 12, Chapter 6, Bhakti-Sufi Traditions, pp. 155–157; Dileep Karanth, Amir Khusrau's Contributions to Indian Music: A Preliminary Survey, Sangeet Natak, 2008. Online sources consulted 25 November 2026.]

body:
Meaning of a gharana

The word gharana is derived from the word ghar, meaning house or household. In Hindustani classical music, a gharana is an established musical lineage recognised for its distinctive approach to musical presentation and the transmission of knowledge.

A gharana may develop around a prominent musician, a musical family or a geographical centre. Its distinctive style is preserved and transmitted across generations.

Membership of a gharana does not necessarily require a biological relationship with its founding family. A disciple who learns its musical tradition may also become an exponent of that gharana.

Guru-shishya parampara

The guru-shishya parampara is the traditional teacher-disciple system through which musical knowledge, compositions and stylistic principles are transmitted.

Gharanas developed partly through this system of sustained training. A disciple learns an inherited style and may subsequently transmit it to another generation.

Important Hindustani vocal gharanas

GharanaHistorical centreRepresentative exponents
GwaliorGwalior, Madhya PradeshHassu Khan, Haddu Khan, Omkarnath Thakur
AgraAgra, Uttar PradeshFaiyaz Khan
KiranaKairana, Uttar PradeshAbdul Karim Khan, Bhimsen Joshi
Jaipur-AtrauliJaipur and AtrauliAlladiya Khan, Kishori Amonkar
PatialaPatiala, PunjabBade Ghulam Ali Khan
Rampur-SahaswanRampur and Sahaswan, Uttar PradeshInayat Hussain Khan

Distinguishing features

  • Gwalior: Widely regarded as the oldest established Khayal gharana. It has played an important role in the dissemination of Khayal music.
  • Agra: Shows a strong historical influence of Dhrupad on Khayal singing.
  • Kirana: Particularly associated with careful treatment of musical notes and melodic development.
  • Jaipur-Atrauli: Known for its distinctive repertoire, including complex and less commonly performed ragas.
  • Patiala: Associated with expressive and agile vocal presentation.
  • Rampur-Sahaswan: An important lineage of Khayal singing associated with the musical centres of Rampur and Sahaswan.

Instrumental gharanas

The gharana system is not restricted to vocal music. Instrumental traditions also develop distinctive lineages.

The Maihar gharana is particularly associated with the instrumental music tradition developed by Allauddin Khan. Its prominent musicians include sitar exponent Ravi Shankar and sarod exponent Ali Akbar Khan.

The Senia tradition traces its musical heritage to Tansen. The name Senia is derived from his name and is associated with several instrumental lineages.

Tabla music also has recognised gharanas, traditionally including Delhi, Ajrada, Lucknow, Farrukhabad, Banaras and Punjab.

A gharana is a musical lineage, whereas Khayal is a vocal form and a raga is a melodic framework. These categories describe different aspects of music.

Gujarat connection

Gujarat has contributed to the development and transmission of several Hindustani gharanas. Pandit Omkarnath Thakur was an important exponent of the Gwalior tradition. Faiyaz Khan of the Agra gharana served as a court musician in Baroda, while Abdul Karim Khan of the Kirana gharana also received Baroda patronage.

Prelims focus

  • Gwalior is widely regarded as the oldest established Khayal gharana.
  • Agra gharana: Faiyaz Khan; Kirana gharana: Abdul Karim Khan.
  • Jaipur-Atrauli gharana: Alladiya Khan.
  • Patiala gharana: Bade Ghulam Ali Khan.
  • Maihar gharana: Allauddin Khan and his instrumental lineage.
  • Trap: A gharana need not consist exclusively of members of the same family.

[References: NIOS, Indian Culture and Heritage, Secondary Course 223, Chapter 12, section on Hindustani music; Darbar, The Vocal Gharana System of Hindustani Classical Music; The Indian Music Archive, Gharanas and Lineages; Pustakalaya, Volume 9, Sangita Natya, Chapter 7, section 7.3; Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda, Faculty of Performing Arts, Contribution of Artists in the Development of Gharanas of Vocal Music, p. 93; Gujarat Government, NRI Division, Dance and Music. Consulted 25 November 2026.]
